title: How great stocks drop 50% | John Huber
description:
John Huber is the portfolio manager of Saber Capital Management, which he founded in 2013 after a journalism degree and about eight years buying foreclosed real estate from banks around the financial crisis. He runs Saber as a family partnership modeled on Buffett’s partnership of the 1950s.

This discussion took place live on October 23rd, 2026, on the MicroCapClub Community. Join MicroCapClub and unlock the ability to listen and participate live in these discussions - https://microcapclub.com/#join 

In this episode, John explains why he moved away from never selling great businesses. He uses Copart to show how a stock at 40 to 50 times earnings can fall 50% on a small hiccup. He also covers how he splits his portfolio between long-term compounders and a basket of Ben Graham-style bargains, how Pitney Bowes moved from one bucket to the other, and how he sizes positions so no single mistake can do serious damage. The conversation opens with his essay on the Tampa Bay Rays and what happens when everyone optimizes for the same metric.

summary: The video argues that high-quality companies can become fully valued or overvalued as market focus shifts, citing Google and Microsoft as examples of stocks that have moved from cheap valuations to premium multiples. The speaker specifically warns that Copart (CPRT) is currently overvalued at 40-50 times earnings and faces competitive pressures, suggesting it could drop 50% if a small hiccup occurs. Consequently, the speaker advises selling Copart while treating other great quality companies as neutral examples of valuation expansion.

claims.claim: The speaker views Copart as a great business that is currently overvalued and facing competitive pressures, warning that a small hiccup could cause the stock to drop 50%.
claims.quote: And so, you know, a stock like Copart is a great example where it's a great business, but if it trades at 40 or 50 times earnings when everything is clicking, all businesses end up going through some hiccup, right? And Copart's gone through a hiccup, right? They're facing some competitive pressures. And whenever there's even a minor hiccup, if the stock is overvalued, my experience and my takeaway from, you know, those those learning lessons is all it takes is a small hiccup for for a stock to drop 50% when it's when it's trading at that level.
claims.speaker: John Huber

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Google was once undervalued at 15 times earnings but is now fully valued, serving as an example of how market focus shifts.
claims.quote: a lot of these great businesses were really undervalued and you know Google traded at 15 times earnings at one point and Apple was 10 times earnings, Microsoft 10 times earnings and these great quality companies became you know huge home runs and the concept of like return on capital and you know terms like capital-l like compounders and things like that everybody became very enamored with these companies for good reasons and originally I think they were very undervalued but they became I think to the point where they're now full fully valued in in general right there's always exceptions but people started prioritizing returns on capital and sort of some in some ways I think forgot what it is they're trying to do which is to compound their capital right so if you pay too much for a good business that might not that might not mean that might not lead to a good investment so that's sort of the the moral of that story, I guess.
